item.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
item.description: The DOJ's embrace of fair use for AI training breaks with the White House's own framework, as OpenAI, Microsoft and news groups battle over copyright.
item.content:encoded:
One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

item.title: Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith to join Wu-Tang Clan for Lions' Thanksgiving halftime show
item.description: Chad Smith, Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer and Bloomfield Hills native, will fly the W with Wu-Tang Clan at halftime of the Detroit Lions Thanksgiving game.
item.content:encoded:
This Thanksgiving, NFL fans will once again have the opportunity to enjoy three games spread across the afternoon and evening.

The Detroit Lions will open the day with their traditional early afternoon matchup, hosting the Chicago Bears. The Cowboys will follow with their long-running home game in the late-afternoon window on Fox. The third game of the day will be played at the new Highmark Stadium, where the Buffalo Bills will host the Kansas City Chiefs.

Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees Wu-Tang Clan will headline the Lions-Bears halftime show.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The legendary hip-hop group will be joined by Red Hot Chili Peppers drummer Chad Smith.

The Lions announced Smith’s special guest appearance Friday.

Detroit rapper Eminem and his manager, Paul Rosenberg, serves as the executive producers of the Lions’ Thanksgiving Day halftime show.

Friday’s announcement marked the second year of their three-year deal to oversee the event. Last year’s performance featured Jack White and a surprise appearance by Eminem.

BUFFALO BILLS TAP HOMETOWN HEROES GOO GOO DOLLS FOR THANKSGIVING NIGHT HALFTIME CONCERT

The Lions have been an NFL Thanksgiving Day staple nearly every season since 1934.

Country music artist Miranda Lambert is scheduled to put on a show at the Cowboys-Eagles matchup later that afternoon.

Last month, the Bills announced the Goo Goo Dolls will perform during halftime of their Thanksgiving night game on Nov. 26. The rock band was originally formed in Buffalo.

"The Goo Goo Dolls halftime performance will take place on the Bills Legends Deck, creating a unique concert experience that can be seen throughout the stadium," the Bills said in a statement. "Fans will also receive PixMob light-up bracelets at their seats, transforming the crowd into an interactive part of the show with synchronized lighting effects throughout Highmark Stadium."

item.title: Nick Saban names three teams above Alabama as college football's true national championship contenders
item.description: Nick Saban says Georgia, Utah and Notre Dame have "the right stuff" in 2026, leaving his former Alabama Crimson Tide off his elite list of three teams.
item.content:encoded:
Nick Saban isn't playing favorites. The former Alabama football head coach said he is not convinced this year’s team has what it takes to make a deep run in this year's College Football Playoff.

During an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show," Saban identified the teams he believes belong in a tier above the rest of the national championship hopefuls. The seven-time national championship-winning coach pointed to Georgia, Utah and Notre Dame as the teams he views as true contenders.

Alabama was notably not included in that group.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Me personally, I think there's three teams that have the right stuff," Saban said. "This is no disrespect to Alabama because I think there's probably seven or eight teams that could win the championship, Alabama being one of them, but if you're a betting man and you say, who can run the ball, who can play good defense, and who has a good quarterback?"

Saban acknowledged that teams outside his top three could still make a run, but he believes each has a potential weakness to overcome.

"You would say Georgia has that, Utah has that. Notre Dame has that. Everybody else maybe has a flaw somewhere along the way. They might be able to overcome it, but I think those three teams have the right stuff."

ESPN DISMISSES UTAH UTES AS NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP CONTENDERS DESPITE BIG WIN OVER BYU: 'THEY WON'T WIN'

Alabama has built a respectable resume this season. The Crimson Tide have knocked off two ranked teams, Kentucky and South Carolina. They also took Georgia down to the wire in a close loss at home. Since dropping games to the Bulldogs and the Tennessee Volunteers, Alabama has put together a three-game winning streak against SEC opponents.

After the College Football Playoff selection committee released its third rankings earlier this week, chair Hunter Yurachek pointed to Alabama’s overall profile, including its margin of victory.

"I think it's a collection of things for Alabama," Yurachek said. "Not only the margin of wins, their SEC wins, which is close to 23 points a game, but their relative scoring defense is in the top 20, relative scoring offense is in the top five, record strength is in the top 5. Quite honestly, when we watch them on film, when we watch their games, we really feel like they're one of the best three or four teams in the country."'

While Saban offered his assessment Friday, Kalen DeBoer struck a more optimistic tone about Alabama in his third season leading the program.

"I feel like we're more complete as a football team and able to play anybody, anytime, anywhere," DeBoer said. "But you got to go do it."

item.title: LSU women's basketball star MiLaysia Fulwiley faces only misdemeanor charges after arrest
item.description: LSU's MiLaysia Fulwiley faces only misdemeanor fleeing and resisting charges after her arrest, with felony counts dropped and a diversion program planned.
item.content:encoded:
LSU women’s basketball player MiLaysia Fulwiley will face misdemeanor traffic citations stemming from a recent traffic incident.

The felony charges included in her initial booking will now be pursued as misdemeanor counts, the East Baton Rouge District Attorney's Office confirmed Friday. Authorities allege Fulwiley attempted to evade officers during a traffic stop.

District Attorney Hillar Moore said fleeing and resisting an officer would be weighed as misdemeanors. Fulwiley will also be referred to a diversion program to resolve the charges. The initial charges listed at the time of Fulwiley’s booking included aggravated battery and assault, based on allegations that she drove her vehicle into an officer’s vehicle. Fulwiley has denied the police's account.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

State police captain Russell Graham said Friday that his agency reviewed evidence with Moore and agreed with his decision. "After a thorough review with all involved parties, the charges were amended based on the circumstances and evidence presented," State Police said in a written statement provided by Graham.

Fulwiley has not appeared in a game for LSU since her arrest. It remains unclear whether she will return to the team.

ALABAMA DISMISSES DEFENSIVE BACK DRE KIRKPATRICK JR FROM TEAM AFTER BEING ARRESTED FOR SECOND TIME

Fulwiley apologized to police and her teammates.

"Saturday night ended in a situation that never should have happened," she said in a statement released by LSU. "I owe an apology to the officers involved and everyone who calls themselves a Tiger. I also want to apologize to my family and all those who love and support me."

The traffic stop happened near Tiger Stadium in Baton Rouge as the a football game between LSU and Texas was ending.

"Rules and laws apply to everyone, including the instructions of officers working a game night in Baton Rouge," Fulwiley said. "I respect the job those officers do, and I’ll let the legal process run its course. My focus is doing what this program asks of me and earning back the trust of the people who count on me."

Fulwiley scored a season-high 23 points on Nov. 13 during LSU’s 101-37 win over the University of Denver.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Mets offer superstar Tarik Skubal the largest pitcher contract in baseball history: report
item.description: The New York Mets have reportedly offered Tarik Skubal a nine-year deal near $400 million that would shatter Yoshinobu Yamamoto's record pitcher contract.
item.content:encoded:
The offseason is early, but the New York Mets have reportedly made history.

The Mets have offered superstar pitcher Tarik Skubal a nine-year contract that is just short of $400 million, according to MLB Network Radio analyst Jim Duquette. Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander currently have the highest annual average value of any pitcher in MLB history at $43. 3 million, and the Mets' reported offer would exceed that.

Los Angeles Dodgers ace Yoshinobu Yamamoto currently has the largest contract for a pitcher in MLB history, with a 12-year, $325 million contract, and Skubal's reported offer would shatter that.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Mets owner Steve Cohen met with Skubal in California last week and is expected to be all in on signing the 30-year-old, according to the New York Post. The team's reported offer of about $400 million would certainly qualify as "all in."

Skubal has also met with the Dodgers, with whom he finished the 2026 season after being traded by the Detroit Tigers at the trade deadline; the San Diego Padres; and the Toronto Blue Jays.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The two-time American League Cy Young winner was once again his usual self with the Tigers and Dodgers last year. In 26 starts, he went 12-7 with a 2.72 ERA in 158 2/3 innings pitched. He missed 38 days in May and June after undergoing arthroscopic surgery to remove loose bodies in his elbow.

In 2024, the two-time All-Star went 18-4 with a 2.39 ERA in 192 innings pitched. In 2025, he had a 13-6 record with a 2.21 ERA in 195 1/3 innings pitched and won the Cy Young both seasons. Skubal spent his entire career with the Tigers before being traded at the deadline.

Wherever and whenever Skubal signs, he will become a very, very rich man.

item.title: Alabama woman pleads guilty after reportedly using smart glasses to target drug trial witnesses
item.description: Tierra Shatalia Douglas pleaded guilty to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness after targeting people who testified in a federal drug trial.
item.content:encoded:
An Alabama woman accused of using Meta smart glasses to secretly record witnesses in a federal drug trial has pleaded guilty.

Tierra Shatalia Douglas, 36, on Thursday admitted to conspiracy to retaliate against a witness in the January prosecution of Glennie "Little Man" McGee and his wife, Echandza Maxie, according to local outlet AL.

The couple, along with Maxie’s sister, Exavieria Maxie, were involved in a multimillion-dollar drug trafficking organization that distributed bulk cocaine and fentanyl and used children as couriers, according to the Justice Department.

DRUG RING BUSTED, ILLEGAL ALIENS CUFFED BY HOMELAND SECURITY TASK FORCE IN SOUTH CAROLINA: DOJ

In the eight months following the prosecution, Douglas repeatedly harassed the witnesses and attempted to obtain their personal information before her arrest in September.

"Douglas disseminated the videos to publicly identify and intimidate the witnesses," court records said, according to AL.

The harassment included secretly recording witnesses as they left the courthouse after testifying, according to Fox10TV.

On Jan. 16, one of the witnesses said he received a video from a friend showing him exiting the courtroom after testifying, the outlet reported.

'SEE A TRUE HOLOCAUST': RELIGION PROFESSOR INDICTED AFTER ANONYMOUS ANTISEMITIC POSTS EXPOSED

In one of the videos she recorded of a witness, Douglas asked someone whether they recognized him, saying, "This guy telling, do anyone know him, he needs to be hurt," according to AL.

She also used ChatGPT to generate and distribute a flyer identifying one of the witnesses as a "snitch," the outlet said.

Reports added that Douglas sent Discord messages identifying one of the witness's minor children and the school the child attended.

In one case, Douglas allegedly sent text messages to a witness she had saved in her phone contacts as "The Rat," taunting him repeatedly for testifying.

Douglas reportedly confessed after officials confronted her with evidence that included internal surveillance footage from the courthouse.

Douglas was arrested in September and pleaded guilty Thursday.

Her sentencing is set for February 2027, according to reports.

She faces a maximum sentence of life in prison, though prosecutors reportedly agreed to recommend leniency, reports say.

item.title: New drug combo shrinks tumors in most patients facing aggressive cancer type
item.description: The pancreatic cancer pill daraxonrasib shrank tumors in 60.7% of patients when paired with chemotherapy, and 8.2% saw tumors vanish on scans.
item.content:encoded:
Pairing an experimental pill with standard chemotherapy shrank tumors or halted growth in most patients with advanced pancreatic cancer, according to early clinical trial results presented Friday at a major international cancer conference.

The findings, shared at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium in Barcelona, come from a phase ½ trial testing a daily oral medication called daraxonrasib, along with two standard intravenous chemotherapy drugs, gemcitabine and nab-paclitaxel.

The trial focused on 61 patients whose pancreatic cancer had already spread to other organs and who had not yet received treatment for their advanced disease.

PANCREATIC CANCER PATIENT BEN SASSE SEES 'MASSIVE' TUMOR REDUCTION WITH EXPERIMENTAL NEW DRUG

Pancreatic cancer is notoriously difficult to treat because more than half of patients are diagnosed after the disease has already spread, research shows.

In major clinical trials for metastatic pancreatic cancer, chemotherapy alone shrinks tumors in about 23% to 42% of patients, but the disease typically begins growing again after five to six months, and most patients survive between 8 and 11 months.

According to National Cancer Institute data, only about 3% of patients with distant-stage disease live five years past diagnosis.

In the new study, which tracked patients for a median follow-up of 18 months, tumors shrank in 60.7% of cases, including 8.2% where they disappeared entirely on scans. Overall, the combination stopped tumor growth in 90.2% of participants.

FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Patients went a median of 12.8 months before their cancer worsened, almost double the timeframe typically seen with standard chemotherapy, and 76.6% were still alive at the one-year mark, the study found.

"We are now seeing not only substantial tumor shrinkages, including complete responses, but also durable disease control, with median progression-free survival exceeding one year," study lead Dr. Wungki Park, a gastrointestinal medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, said in a press release.

More than 90% of pancreatic cancers are driven by a faulty gene called RAS, which allows tumors to keep growing. Daraxonrasib is designed to turn off that growth signal, something scientists long thought was impossible to fix with medication.

Dr. Elena Garralda, chair of the symposium and co-director of the clinical research program at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology in Spain, who was not involved in the research, said the results show that RAS-targeted drugs can be combined with existing treatments at the start of treatment to potentially achieve longer-lasting benefits.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Side effects included rash, diarrhea, fatigue and low blood cell counts linked to chemotherapy, most of which were manageable with standard care.

Only 5% of patients stopped treatment because of side effects tied to daraxonrasib.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Researchers emphasized that the findings carry some limitations.

Because this was an early-phase, single-group study involving 61 people, all participants received the experimental combination. Without a direct comparison group of patients receiving standard chemotherapy alone, doctors cannot yet confirm how much better the new regimen performs or whether it definitively extends overall survival.

The findings also apply strictly to metastatic pancreatic cancer, even though RAS mutations drive several other cancers, including certain lung, colorectal and gynecological cancers. Separate studies would be needed to test whether the combination works in those diseases.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

The trial was funded by Revolution Medicines, the California-based developer of daraxonrasib.

To determine whether these early findings translate into a durable survival benefit, researchers have launched a larger, randomized Phase 3 trial, called RASolute-303, which directly compares daraxonrasib — both on its own and combined with chemotherapy — against standard chemotherapy alone.

item.title: 'Enough': Protesters decry antisemitism after Hunter College student event including Jewish group is canceled
item.description: Pro-Israel rally organizers at Hunter College say the cancelled Cultural Arts Night shows antisemitism at CUNY, as counter protesters chant nearby.
item.content:encoded:
A crowd gathered Thursday outside Hunter College to protest after the school's student government seemingly canceled an event due to the participation of a Jewish organization.

On one side of the street, pro-Israel protesters chanted "enough is enough" and waved American and Israeli flags as speakers addressed the crowd. Across the street, a group of counter-protesters gathered waving Palestinian flags while yelling chants of their own. 

Passersby also shouted, some in support and others yelling "Free Palestine" and "F--- Israel."

JEWISH CAMPUS LIFE AT A ‘CROSSING POINT’ AS STUDENTS WEIGH ANTISEMITISM RISKS, NEW REPORT SHOWS

Organizers behind the Stand with Jewish Students at Hunter rally included the Israeli American Council (IAC), Students Supporting Israel (SSI) and #EndJewHatred. 

On flyers advertising the rally, they criticized the college's administration for not doing enough in response to what they saw as an act of antisemitism.

"We're saying enough to the marginalization of the Jewish community. We're saying enough is enough to discrimination against Jewish students. And we're saying enough is enough to this obsessive hatred of all of the symbols of Jewish life, whether it's Hillel on campus or the State of Israel," IAC CEO Elan Carr told Fox News Digital, referring to a chapter of the Jewish student group. 

Michelle Ahdoot, director of programming and strategy at #EndJewHatred, told Fox News Digital the cancellation of the event demonstrated a problem that went beyond Hunter College.

"When a multicultural event is canceled simply because Jewish students are included, we have a serious problem that goes far beyond one event at Hunter College," Ahdoot said. "The very purpose of multiculturalism is to celebrate diversity and inclusion, not to allow certain groups to decide who is welcome and who is not. 

"Any student organization has the right to choose not to participate," he continued. "But when an elected student government responds by canceling the entire event rather than standing up for the inclusion of Jewish students, it sends a dangerous message that Jewish participation is somehow unacceptable."

The Cultural Arts Night was scheduled to take place Nov. 16 but was canceled just days before. Hunter College Undergraduate Student Government (USG) flyers promoting the event showed that clubs involved included Students for Justice in Palestine, the Peruvian Student Association, Hunter Chinese Student & Scholar Association, the Taiwanese Student Association and Hunter Hillel, according to screenshots posted online.

Hillel International is a Jewish organization that can be found on college campuses across the globe. It describes itself as "a space for all kinds of Jewish students — a place where they feel welcomed and included." While its vision includes helping students make "an enduring commitment to Jewish life, learning and Israel," it is focused on Jewish life and culture, hosting holidays and holding events.

FIRE ALARM DISRUPTS NORTHWESTERN 'OCTOBER 7' PLAY BASED ON MASSACRE SURVIVOR TESTIMONY

Rita Levine Rabin Hillel at Hunter College said in a statement on Instagram it was "looking forward" to the event and that it "had no role in the decision to cancel."

"Antisemitism has no place at Hunter College. Jewish students should never be singled out, scapegoated, or made to feel unwelcome because of who they are and the anti-Semitic response online to the cancellation notice has been egregious and inappropriate," the statement read.

Ilya Bratman, who serves as executive director at Hillel at Baruch College in New York City, said the cancellation of Cultural Arts Night was a clear case of antisemitism and a sign that things could escalate.

"This is so obvious, and antisemitism has nothing to do with Israel. And that's what the main thing you have to say very loudly. This is about Jew hatred and exclusion," Bratman told Fox News Digital. "It's the first step in the process, which begins with physical exclusion of Jewish students from campuses. 

"And that is what happened in the 1930s. We know this. This is a slower process here in American campuses, and I believe this is going to keep going if we don't step up in a very serious way to stop it."

Hunter College USG announced the cancellation on Nov. 14 in a statement from Hunter College USG President Sumaiya Ahmed and Vice President Ahmad Waraich. The two student leaders claimed that "lapses in communication kept the details of this event from reaching the people at the top."

"We hear what the student body has said, and we have made the decision to cancel the event as it doesn’t align with our values or the values of the students we represent as the Hunter Community. We apologize to the clubs and students who were affected by this instance," a statement posted on Instagram read.

After the announcement, speculation about the reason for the event's cancellation grew, with some pointing to pressure from anti-Israel activists who objected to Hillel's involvement. While this was not directly addressed, Hunter USG appeared to deny it in a subsequent statement in which it said that the event was canceled over "safety concerns."

BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES

Hunter College is a public institution in the City University of New York (CUNY) system, making allegations of discrimination particularly serious since public schools are legally barred from discriminating based on religion or national origin.

Hunter College told Fox News Digital it was "deeply troubled by reports that some student groups pulled from the event because of Hillel’s participation" and said it was investigating the issue.

"There is no place for discrimination and harassment in our college community. We have policies in place to safeguard that principle and will not hesitate to enforce them," the college said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Michal Mari, who is president of SSI at Hunter College, told Fox News Digital during the rally that the environment at the school has been "tough" for Jewish students. She said Jewish students had seen calls for violence against their community, including statements calling to "bring the war home" and "globalize the intifada." 

Mari believes the cancellation came after clubs dropped out of the event due to Hillel's participation, which she said was "blatant discrimination against Jewish students on campus."

"I've had professors turn their backs to me while I was speaking to them because they found out that I was wearing a Star of David or that I've been to Israel," Mari told Fox News Digital. "So, it's certainly not the most divided, but it's a place where there's work to be done."

Mari addressed the crowd at Thursday night's rally along with a number of other pro-Israel and Jewish speakers, including Shai Davidai, Ari Ackerman, Shabbos Kestenbaum and Rami Matan Even-Esh (also known as Kosha Dillz), among others, including Hunter College students.

Jayne Zirkle, who serves as director of communications for #EndJewHatred, said the organization was "incredibly proud" of the students who chose to speak publicly despite the pressures they face on campus.

"Their courage matters, and they deserve to know they are not standing alone," Zirkle said.

Davidai, a former Columbia University professor, told Fox News Digital he attended the rally to bring attention to what he saw as the "symptom" of a bigger issue.

"The symptom of canceling an event because a Jewish organization is part of it, that is a problem. And, by the way, it's a problem not just for Jews, it's a problem for everyone. Because when you cancel an event, everyone, Jewish or non-Jews, don't get to go to that event," Davidai said.

LEO TERRELL TAKES TRUMP ADMINISTRATION'S ANTISEMITISM FIGHT NATIONWIDE ON 15-CITY TOUR

While Davidai focused on the broader cultural fallout on campus, Kestenbaum, a former Harvard Divinity School student who sued Harvard over campus antisemitism, framed the issue around civil rights law and public funding.

"You cannot violate civil rights law. Colleges don't get to pick and choose which statute of the Civil Rights Act they want to subscribe to. There is one standard for all universities across the country, and if those universities insist on discriminating against students because of their ethnicity or because of their religious identity, that is illegal," Kestenbaum told Fox News Digital.

Kestenbaum is not the only one who has brought up the possible legal issues with canceling the event. New York City Council Member Eric Dinowitz publicly called for a civil rights investigation.

"[Hunter College] USG cancels a multicultural arts event because it did not align with its 'values.' It appears to be yet another chapter in the troubling history of antisemitism at CUNY and Hunter," Dinowitz wrote on X. "That's why [CUNY] must immediately launch a Title VI investigation."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Along with calls for institutional and legal accountability, speakers at Thursday night's rally encouraged students at Hunter College not to retreat from campus life and stay silent.

"Every student at Hunter or anywhere else, if you speak up, and when you speak up, we've got your back," Davidai said in an interview with Fox News Digital. 

"We've got your back with numbers. We've got your back with legal support. We got your back on social media. We have got your backs. But it's up to you to speak up, because if you don't speak up then, you know, the word doesn't come out."

Mari echoed the message, saying that the Jewish community at Hunter College was ready to rally behind those who choose to speak out.

"Courage isn't lack of fear but acting in the face of fear," Mari told Fox News Digital. "You have a community behind you. The Jewish community, especially, is one that is always behind you."

Hunter USG and Hunter Hillel did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

item.title: Charlie Sheen stunned to learn fellow actor Rob Lowe had been praying for him for years
item.description: Rob Lowe revealed on Charlie Sheen's "Mostly Sheenius" podcast that he prayed for the actor for years while struggling with his own sobriety, calling him "my guy" in recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Actors Charlie Sheen and Rob Lowe, both of whom struggled with addiction in the past, shared a moment on Sheen’s podcast when Lowe revealed he had been praying for Sheen for years.

Sheen spoke with Lowe on his "Mostly Sheenius" podcast. Lowe has had his own addiction struggles in the past and stars in the new film "Confession," a historical drama set in the Soviet Union in 1938.

"I’d like to clear the air," Sheen said. "I’d like to, you know, not pretend like something didn't happen or whatever. I think it's juvenile, and I don't think — I think it's how we grow for sure, you know, is to just be honest. 

"And I've sent a few tweets, back when they were tweets, just some stuff about you that was really unkind and unfair." 

CHARLIE SHEEN HAS BLUNT RESPONSE TO QUESTIONS ABOUT HIS HEALTH AND FINANCES

When Lowe signaled that he didn't care about the past social media posts, Sheen replied, "OK, but I do."

"They were mean and stupid, and it was all before Dec. 12, 2017," Sheen added. "That's when I got off the dope and quit the booze and all that s---, you know. So, anyway, I just wanted to offer that."

"Well, thank you, thank you," Lowe said, saying that even if the tweets made it to his newsfeed, "I forgot about them. And if they did, I probably just went, ‘Well, that's, you know, Charlie's — one day he's going to he's going to get it.’ Which you did."

Sheen is a major public figure not only for his acting career, but for his controversies and his rocky road to sobriety after years of addiction. 

Sheen’s 2025 Netflix documentary series featured him after seven years of sobriety, candidly discussing "his rise to fame and public downfall, joined by family and friends who share untold stories of his journey."

TOM HANKS' SON CHET HANKS SHARES THE LIFE-CHANGING DECISION THAT FOLLOWED REHAB AND ADDICTION

After Sheen recalled Lowe being at his first intervention years ago, Lowe revealed he had been praying for him for years.

"I know you're not a huge, like, program guy. It saved my life, but that's neither here nor there," Lowe said. "But in the program, as you know, they always say, ‘Take a moment of prayer for the alcoholic who still suffers.’ And you were always my guy," Lowe revealed. "Every time, years and years and years."

"So, you were kind of giving that prayer for a couple decades?" Sheen said in surprise.

"Every time. Every time. Every f---ing meeting I went to, bro!, Lowe said.

item.title: USDA releases decades of Bigfoot files, including 1982 Forest Service investigation in Washington state
item.description: The USDA's Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records include an official 1982 Forest Service probe into footprints in Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration has slowly released a trove of government documents about one of the biggest and most enduring mysteries in American folklore: Bigfoot.

On Oct. 15, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) released three files from its "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," The Washington Post first reported, adding fresh intrigue to the legend of the towering, hair-covered creature said to roam North American forests without ever being captured.

NASA CHIEF PULLS BACK CURTAIN ON TRUMP UFO FILES AFTER BIZARRE FINDS SURFACE IN BURIED FED RECORDS

The records include an official U.S. Forest Service (USFS) investigation from June 1982 into reported Bigfoot footprints discovered in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington state's Umatilla National Forest.

Investigators documented track measurements, took color photographs and made plaster casts across several field sites to preserve the unusual physical evidence.

NEW JERSEY COUPLE REPORT SEEING 8-FOOT TALL BIGFOOT STEPPING OUT IN FRONT OF THEIR CAR: 'WE KNOW WHAT WE SAW'

Another file details a reported encounter with the creature in Montana dating back to the 1940s. Separately, USFS staff once hosted a Bigfoot in Your Backyard forum in California's Stanislaus National Forest to discuss local sightings, noting at the time the agency could neither confirm nor deny the creature's existence.

A six-page document included in last month's release, which was written in 1980, recounts a historical report from Petty Creek, Montana, by Leo Kinney, who described spotting a large set of tracks alongside three hunters in the 1940s.

FOLLOW US ON X

"At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn't confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs," Kinney wrote.

The release also includes details of a 2003 sighting in Sanders County, Montana.

IDAHO DEER HUNTER REPORTS BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER IN REMOTE WOODS AFTER HE 'SMELLS THE SMELL'

In an interview with The Washington Post, Jeremiah Byron of the "Bigfoot Society" questioned the timing of the federal disclosures.

"Why is all this cryptid and Bigfoot-related stuff happening now?" Byron asked. "I’m hoping what this means is that they could be ramping up government entities to start releasing information."

While Bigfoot lore has traditionally centered on the Pacific Northwest, the creature has also surfaced in pop culture, with players reporting sightings in the video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

Gamers have shared clips of the cryptid wandering the woods of Leonida, a fictional U.S. state based on Florida, before sprinting away in a panic when spotted, according to GameSpot.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the U.S. Forest Service for comment.

item.title: Zoo shares autopsy findings following Fiona the hippo’s heartbreaking death
item.description: Cincinnati Zoo’s director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger, said a postmortem examination has revealed where the hat was lodged inside Fiona’s digestive tract.
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Zoo on Friday released new autopsy findings after the death of Fiona, the hippo whose battle after swallowing a visitor's hat left people across the nation heartbroken.

A postmortem examination determined that a foreign object, confirmed to be a hat zoo officials said was accidentally thrown into her enclosure, was lodged deep inside the hippo's massive digestive tract, according to the zoo's director of animal health, Dr. Mike Wenninger.

The hat was located halfway through the small intestine, about 25 feet from the beginning of her intestinal tract and 50 feet from where it would have exited her body as waste.

FIONA THE HIPPO HONORED BY US SENATE IN UNANIMOUS RESOLUTION PRAISING CINCINNATI ZOO STAFF

The findings settle lingering questions about the hat's exact location after care teams spent days trying to locate it using various methods, including ultrasounds and upper and lower gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopies.

Care teams even obtained 9-foot-long endoscopy tools but were still unable to reach her intestines through her mouth.

"The upper GI endoscopy couldn't even reach out of her large sacculated stomach," Wenninger said.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

"Given her anatomy and the attachments from her intestinal tract to body wall, there's no place, no way to get in there with specialized endoscopes," he added.

The hat's location and Fiona's anatomy also made surgical removal impossible, Wenninger said, explaining that even laparoscopic procedures, in which a scope is inserted into the abdomen through a small incision, were not feasible.

"Laparoscopic surgery wasn't possible given the location and a laparotomy, so (an) open incision in a hippo that size with an incision that's that long would have been a death sentence for her," he said.

Zoo officials added that the findings confirm the care team did everything possible, and the complications left no viable options for additional operations.

"No treatment aside from supportive care had any chance for success, and the necropsy confirmed that no amount of supportive care would have worked," Wenninger said.

Following Fiona's death, the facility said the zoo remains open, but the area around the Hippo Cove enclosure will be closed through the weekend to give the animal care team the space it needs during this time.

"Keepers, vets, staff and volunteers are shaken and trying to navigate this loss. She meant a lot to a lot of people," the zoo said in a statement.

FUN FACT: FIONA THE HIPPO BECAME THE SMALLEST NILE HIPPO KNOWN TO SURVIVE

While most hippos in captivity live up to 50 years, Fiona was just 9 years old when her condition rapidly deteriorated in November.

She first made headlines in 2017 after defying the odds as a premature hippo. She was born six weeks early, weighing just 29 pounds. By comparison, healthy newborn hippos typically weigh between 50 and 120 pounds at birth.

Zoo officials said Fiona became ill after a visitor tossed a hat into the air near her enclosure. The hat became caught in a ceiling fan, which propelled it over the viewing windows.

EL-SAYED RALLYGOERS URGE 'MAJOR CHANGE', CASH HANDOUTS TO FIGHT COST CRISIS

LOCALS OF MICHIGAN CITY WITH LARGEST MUSLIM POPULATION BELIEVE AMERICA SHOULD LOOK MORE LIKE DEARBORN

NYC'S MAMDANI SAYS ABDUL EL-SAYED'S SENATE VICTORY IN MICHIGAN 'MEANS SO MUCH TO SO MANY'

ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE

EL-SAYED’S LIBERAL AGENDA CLASHES WITH MUSLIM VOTERS WHO BACK HIM ANYWAY: ‘MALE VERSION’ OF ILHAN OMAR

Immigrants from Lebanon, Iraq and Syria began settling in the Detroit area in the early 20th century, drawn in part by growing demand for labor in the auto industry.

DETROIT PISTONS TO HOST MUSLIM NIGHT WITH EL-SAYED SHOUTOUT, GAZA DONATIONS; NO CHRISTIAN-FOCUSED EVENT

JEWISH LEADERS IN MICHIGAN PREPARE TO WORK WITH ABDUL EL-SAYED DESPITE LINGERING CONCERNS

The nearby city of Warren, Michigan, another Detroit suburb, has also experienced demographic changes. The sale of a local church for conversion into the Al Ihsaan Islamic Center reflects one such change.

BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE'

Warren, Michigan's third-largest city after Detroit and Grand Rapids, grew rapidly during the post-World War II auto manufacturing boom, as war veterans moved to the area to work for Ford and General Motors. The blue-collar, white-picket-fence community incorporated as a city in 1957.

item.title: Texas Gov-elect Gina Hinojosa vows to rescind Abbott's H-1B visa restrictions despite admitting program abuse
item.description: Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa says she will rescind Greg Abbott's H-1B hiring freeze on day one, even conceding companies have abused the visa program.
item.content:encoded:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) said she plans to rescind Gov. Greg Abbott’s hiring freeze on H-1B visa workers at state agencies and public universities on her first day in office, even as she acknowledged that the federal visa program has been abused.

In a recent interview with the Texas Tribune, Hinojosa, a Democrat, dismissed Abbott’s January directive restricting new H-1B visa petitions as a distraction.

"Yeah, that does not make sense to me. I will tell you, I’m not doing culture wars. That’s not what I was elected to do," Hinojosa said.

Abbott issued the order in January to bar state agencies and public universities from filing new H-1B petitions without written approval from the Texas Workforce Commission, citing reports that employers had displaced U. S. workers with lower-paid foreign labor.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORPEDOES TRUMP’S BID TO PROTECT US JOBS BY REFORMING CONTROVERSIAL IMMIGRATION POLICY

"In the most egregious schemes, employers have even fired American workers and replaced them with H-1B employees, often at lower wages," Abbott wrote in his January directive.

While Hinojosa vowed to scrap the restrictions, she conceded that companies have exploited the visa system.

"There are abuses when it comes to H-1Bs, absolutely," Hinojosa told the Texas Tribune. "Companies should not be getting a bunch of tax breaks for jobs to only then use that money to hire H-1B employees. That’s wrong. That’s happening right now. I don’t support that."

Hinojosa, a Democratic state representative from Austin, defeated Abbott in the Nov. 3 election to deny the three-term Republican incumbent a fourth term, becoming the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990. With Republicans still holding a majority in the Texas Senate, rescinding Abbott’s executive orders offers Hinojosa an immediate way to reshape state policy without legislative approval.

HISTORIC GOP DEFEAT FUELS 11TH-HOUR POWER STRUGGLE AS NEW ALLIES RALLY TO REIN IN INCOMING DEM GOVERNOR

Hinojosa also defended local school districts’ use of H-1B visas to recruit foreign educators, arguing that Texas schools struggle to find domestic teachers. Abbott’s directive, however, applies only to state agencies and public institutions of higher education, not local K-12 school districts.

A representative for Hinojosa did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. 

Abbott’s freeze was scheduled to remain in place through May 31, 2027, to give lawmakers time to pass broader reforms, while requiring affected agencies and universities to report their current H-1B visa holders and efforts to recruit qualified Texas residents.

item.title: 'The View' co-host stunned as Hostin backs Gavin Newsom bypassing victims' families for death row commutations
item.description: Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro were split over Newsom's 548 death row commutations, and Navarro argued that Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the families.
item.content:encoded:
"The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared surprised when co-host Sunny Hostin disagreed with her argument that Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the victims' families before ending the death sentences of 548 inmates in his state.

"I don’t like the way it went through. And I think that before he announced that, he needed to get the approval and agreement of the families of the victims, because the people that he’s commuted the sentences for are people who are on death row. They’re people who committed murder, and I tend to be against blanket pardon to begin with," Navarro said.

Newsom commuted the death sentences of all of California's death-row inmates in early November, effectively ending capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions.

CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE'

"I think these are things you have to take on a case-by-case basis, and I think it’s disrespectful to the victims’ families," Navarro said.

"You can disagree or agree with the death penalty, but to me, if your loved one has been murdered, you have the right to be told that this is happening, before you read about it."

Hostin said, "I disagree with that."

"That the victim's family should have been told?" Navarro asked in response.

"Yes," Hostin repeated. "I'm an opponent of the death penalty. I think that God gives life."

Hostin said those cases were under Newsom's purview as governor. She argued that the system is "broken," and no one should have to pay the ultimate price for a broken system.

ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION

"One innocent person being put to death is not worth the entire system," she said. "And if you look at the system, it's not a deterrent. That the statistics show that more than half of death row exonerees are Black, even though Black people just make up 13.6% of the U.S. population.

"And nearly 60% of the people that are found to have been wrongfully convicted of murder by the Innocence Project are African Americans, and so the system is broken," Hostin continued. "And you should not pay the ultimate price for a system that is broken." 

Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin sided with Navarro, arguing the move was a betrayal of the families.

"It was a betrayal of the families to not notify them beforehand," Griffin said. "People can agree or disagree on the death penalty. It's actually come up as a ballot initiative in California twice in the last decade. And California voters actually voted to keep capital punishment in place.

"I think (Newsom) has the purview to do this, but then to not notify families, that gets in the way of their grief," she added. 

"There's no greater trauma than having a loved one murdered in a brutal way and thinking it's been adjudicated in the court, and there's a certain outcome in finding out in a newspaper, basically, that that's not happening." 

GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029

Griffin also said it could be a political move by Newsom.

"This should have been handled better," she said. "And I think there's a political side to this too. He wants to run for president. He wants to seem more progressive. Kamala Harris may run for president. He's gonna be like, ‘She was a prosecutor who put people in jail.’ So, I don't like it. He should have notified the families." 

Co-host Sara Haines agreed, arguing that undoing all the death sentences treated each case the same.

"I think the point is that if you want to change something going forward, put it on a ballot, and clearly California doesn't want it taken off," she said. "At that point, I think he should have looked case-by-case, because to not reach out to these families, they get nothing back. 

"Any closure they get is small. But some of these people deeply found something in this conviction and this determination. And to just undo it in one blanket swipe is to treat them all the same." 

When reached for comment, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to a letter Newsom issued explaining his decision. 

In part, Newsom wrote, "This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families. I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss.

"I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action," he continued. "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing."

Later in the letter, Newsom said, "California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that. I recognize the limits of this clemency action, which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences. The power to repeal the death penalty rests with the Legislature and voters."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"Victims’ rights were disregarded and trampled by Governor Newsom," Y. David Scharf, chairman of Morrison Cohen LLP, told Fox News Digital in a statement. 

"Whatever one’s view of the death penalty, the families of murder victims deserved more than to learn that the sentences in their loved ones’ cases were being swept away as part of a blanket decision affecting hundreds of cases.

"The governor may have the constitutional authority to commute these sentences, but having the power to do something does not mean the people most profoundly affected by it should be treated as an afterthought," he continued. 

"At a minimum, these families deserved notice, respect and an opportunity to be heard before such a consequential decision was announced."

item.title: Fiona the hippo honored by US Senate in unanimous resolution praising Cincinnati Zoo staff
item.description: Fiona the hippo received a formal Senate tribute from Sen. Bernie Moreno one day after the Cincinnati Zoo Nile hippopotamus died after a medical emergency.
item.content:encoded:
Fiona the hippo received a formal tribute from the U. S. Senate on Friday, one day after the beloved Cincinnati Zoo resident died following a medical emergency.

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, introduced the resolution honoring Fiona's life and legacy while expressing the chamber's gratitude to the zoo's staff for their care and dedication. The measure passed by unanimous consent.

Speaking from the Senate floor next to a photo of the hippopotamus, Moreno described Fiona's death as a "devastating loss" and a tragic accident.

BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT

"The people who come to our city, our state, that now don’t have Fiona there," Moreno said. "It’s going to leave a hole in the zoo and a hole in their heart."

The tribute came one day after the Cincinnati Zoo announced that Fiona died after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her enclosure last week. According to the zoo, a visitor tossed the hat into the air outside the exhibit, where it caught on a ceiling fan and was launched over the viewing windows into her habitat.

"The vet staff tried everything they could to help her after she ingested a hat that ended up in her habitat by accident last week," the zoo said in a Thursday statement. "Despite multiple attempts to move the hat out of her system, it was ultimately too much to overcome."

'WORST AQUARIUM EVER' REVIEW SENDS WHALING MUSEUM'S SALES SOARING 250%

Fiona, a Nile hippopotamus, rose to international fame in January 2017 after she was born six weeks premature, weighing just 29 pounds. Her survival drew millions of followers online and inspired books, clothing, beer and an ice cream flavor.

Tributes poured in across Ohio and Capitol Hill following her death, with Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., praising Fiona on X as a "beloved presence" and the Cincinnati Bengals remembering her as "The queen of the Queen City."

A representative for Moreno's office and the Cincinnati Zoo did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Fox News Digitals' Louis Casiano contributed to this report.

item.title: Verdict reached in Los Angeles retrial over 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people
item.description: Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of federal arson in the Pacific Palisades fire that killed 12 and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes after a mistrial.
item.content:encoded:
A man accused of sparking the deadly 2025 Pacific Palisades wildfire that killed 12 people and destroyed nearly 7,000 homes was found guilty on all counts Friday after a federal retrial in Los Angeles, months after his first trial ended in a mistrial.

Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, a former Uber driver with dual U.S.-French citizenship, had been charged with two federal arson counts — including destruction of property by means of fire — in U.S. District Court. 

He was retried on a scaled-down grand jury indictment after his initial three-week trial ended in a hung jury in June.

Ahead of the second trial, federal prosecutors dropped one of the original three charges against Rinderknecht, and modified the two remaining federal arson counts, reducing his maximum possible prison sentence from 45 years to 40 years.

PALISADES FIRE SUSPECT ALLEGEDLY DRIVEN BY 'SOCIETAL REVENGE,' BEHAVIORAL ANALYST TESTIFIES IN COURT

Following the verdict, a juror in the case — identified only by his first name, Cameron, who served as Juror No. 3 — told reporters that deliberations stretched across roughly two days as the panel systematically reviewed every piece of testimony and video evidence from the first day of court to the last.

"I’ll be honest, I was the person who found him not guilty. Originally, I was the one who stood out on that. So it took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise," he said, noting the initial tally stood at 10 guilty, one not guilty and one undecided.

Cameron said his initial hesitation centered on a "technical review" of the fire investigation and whether investigators properly followed protocol when linking the initial blaze to the later inferno. He said the jury ultimately concluded the defendant's own testimony — placing himself alone on the hill on a clear, calm night while smoking and carrying a lighter — pointed to him starting the first fire, which then smoldered into the Jan. 7 disaster.

"What I will say is that his intent was to start a fire," Cameron said. "What that fire did after his actions, whether he can say or whether no one can say, like who knows? Only he will know and only God himself. And so the result of his fire is what ultimately led to January 7th [2025]."

DEFENSE TEAM TRIES TO TIE NBA CHAMPION CHIS BOSH TO PALISADES ARSONIST CASE, CITING FIREWORK EVIDENCE: REPORT

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said in a statement following the conviction that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured."

"Nearly two years ago, the Palisades Fire devastated our city, taking innocent lives, destroying thousands of homes, and changing so many lives and Los Angeles forever," Bass said. "So many are still struggling to rebuild. For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality. 

"Los Angeles will always stand with Pacific Palisades."

Los Angeles City Councilwoman Traci Park, who represents the Pacific Palisades, said the verdict "puts a bookend on one piece of this saga," though she emphasized that thousands of residents remain displaced and locked in disputes with insurance companies nearly two years later.

"The emotions that come with it really are a mixed bag, because at the end of the day, no amount of courtroom justice will ever restore what was lost or repair the harm that was caused," Park told reporters.

The blaze tore through the seaside enclave of Pacific Palisades, leveling entire neighborhoods and causing property damage estimated between $35 billion and $150 billion.

Federal prosecutors also alleged in court filings that Rinderknecht was partly inspired by Luigi Mangione, who pleaded guilty to federal charges in the December 2024 murder of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York City.

His defense attorney, Steve Haney, argued that prosecutors lacked physical evidence tying his client to arson and contended the massive Jan. 7 blaze was set separately by someone else.

item.title: Drake Maye fractured his fibula, leaving his season and Patriots playoff hopes in doubt: report
item.description: Drake Maye reportedly fractured his fibula in Germany and will miss deep into the season, while A.J. Brown's also suffered a hamstring injury that will force him to miss time.
item.content:encoded:
The New England Patriots' playoff hopes took a massive blow on Friday.

Drake Maye fractured his right fibula in the Patriots' 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Germany, according to ESPN. The 24-year-old will not need surgery on the injured leg, but the injury will sideline him deep into the season and may even end it, according to the report.

The two-time Pro Bowler did not suffer any ligament damage. The bad news didn't stop there for the Patriots, as star wide receiver A.J. Brown is expected to be sidelined for multiple weeks with a hamstring injury he suffered in the team's loss in Germany, according to ESPN's report.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Week 10 loss dropped the Patriots to 5-5 on the season and outside the playoff picture. They trail the 8-1 Buffalo Bills in the AFC East, and it would take a miracle for them to claw back and win the division for the second straight season without Maye and Brown.

The Patriots' five losses this season are already more than they had all of last season, as they went 14-3 en route to representing the AFC in the Super Bowl, which they lost to the Seattle Seahawks.

This season has been much different from the previous one. Before getting hurt in Germany, Maye had not been playing nearly as well. In 2025, Maye completed 72% of his passes (first in the NFL) for 4,394 yards, 31 touchdowns and eight interceptions, while rushing for 450 yards and four touchdowns. He finished second in MVP voting.

In 10 games in 2026, his completion percentage dipped to 65.6%, and he passed for 2,330 yards, 18 touchdowns and 11 interceptions, while rushing for 230 yards and three touchdowns. His play this season is one of the reasons the team has struggled to replicate last season's success.

As for Brown, his hamstring injury will be the third different injury to cause him to miss time in his first season with the Patriots after being traded from the Philadelphia Eagles. The Patriots traded their 2028 first-round pick and a 2027 fifth-round pick for Brown, and the early return on investment has not been good for New England. In four games, Brown has just 11 catches for 128 yards.

The Patriots will turn to backup quarterback Tommy DeVito in Maye's absence, and they will hope the former New York Giants quarterback can salvage their playoff hopes. New England is on their bye week this week.

item.title: Cardinals may start their fourth QB in four weeks as Carson Beck has injury after first career start
item.description: Carson Beck's back spasms could push the Arizona Cardinals to 40-year-old Josh Johnson, their fourth starting quarterback in four weeks, versus the Chiefs.
item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Cardinals quarterback carousel is still spinning.

After just one start, Cardinals rookie Carson Beck is dealing with back spasms and may not play Sunday against the Kansas City Chiefs. If the 25-year-old cannot play, the Cardinals will turn to 40-year-old Josh Johnson.

If Johnson starts, it will be the Cardinals' fourth different starting quarterback in four weeks. Head coach Mike LaFleur reported Friday that they will see how Beck responds to treatment tomorrow, and that he doesn't think Beck will be out multiple weeks.

"You go with the people who know what they’re doing to treat it. It’s not like this is the first time he’s dealt with it," LaFleur said. "We’ll see more tomorrow."

Beck had dealt with back spasms earlier in the season. The former Miami star quarterback went 11 for 18 for 108 yards with two interceptions in the Cardinals' 34-6 loss to the Los Angeles Rams in his first career start Sunday.

For LaFleur, he has familiarity with Johnson, as he was the offensive coordinator with the New York Jets in 2021 and called plays for the journeyman quarterback then.

"Cool part is, if it is Josh, I’ve called plays for him before and had a really great experience calling plays for him," LaFleur said. "So, we’ll go shoot our shot and I expect nothing less from our guys."

If you told Cardinals fans a month ago that the team might be on its fourth different starting quarterback in four weeks, they'd be pretty surprised. In Week 8, the Cardinals started Jacoby Brissett against the Dallas Cowboys. He was benched in the second half for Gardner Minshew II, and the former Jacksonville Jaguars starter led the team to a thrilling comeback.

In the aftermath of that, the Cardinals named Minshew the starting quarterback and traded Brissett to the Baltimore Ravens. In Week 9, Minshew's first start, he suffered a UCL injury that required season-ending surgery.

With Brissett in Baltimore and Minshew hurt, the Cardinals started Beck in Week 10 and now might be turning to Johnson in Week 11. Adding to the chaos, Johnson only joined the Cardinals on Nov. 10, when the team signed him off the Cincinnati Bengals practice squad.

item.title: Knicks star Jalen Brunson reveals how he really feels about 'King of New York' nickname
item.description: Jalen Brunson reacted to "King of New York" talk after leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA title in 53 years during a recent interview.
item.content:encoded:
When you help lead the New York Knicks to its first NBA title in 53 years, in a city that hasn’t seen a "Big Four" team win their championship since the New York Giants in 2011, you get called the "King of New York."

After all, ask anyone around the five boroughs and they’ll tell you: New York City is a basketball town when the Knicks are on top.

Jalen Brunson, the NBA Finals MVP and Knicks superstar point guard, has been hearing "King of New York" thrown around from friends and fans alike since the victory over the San Antonio Spurs this past summer. It’s a moniker synonymous with greatness in a city that begs for it with all its teams and superstar athletes.

To hear it means you’ve accomplished greatness in a city that demands it each season, or else the year is a failure. There’s pressure enough to play in the "World’s Greatest Arena" in Madison Square Garden as the face of the Knicks, but how does Brunson handle being called "King of New York?"

His answer tells you exactly where his mindset is this season, and the many to come.

"To be honest with you, I don’t want to say it’s annoying. It’s more of like when people say that, it’s cool to hear," he told OutKick in a recent interview, while highlighting his partnership with Lowe’s ahead of their big Black Friday activation. "A lot of people who I know, know I don’t like it. So, they’ll just say it to annoy me."

Brunson doesn’t have to explain why he doesn’t like it. The Villanova product has always gone about his business, staying humble and never being boisterous, though he has every reason to be considering what he’s accomplished alongside his Knicks teammates.

Yes, he’s won a championship, perhaps the one title that meant more than the rest in this great city. But his answer says many things, including one isn’t enough.

However, to be called "King of New York" — the same nickname Babe Ruth, Mickey Mantle, Lawrence Taylor, Mark Messier, Eli Manning, Derek Jeter and many others have worn over the years — is something Brunson appreciates.

Even if he doesn’t feel that way himself.

"The one thing that I’ll always think about is when you’re working to achieve something, like a goal to win a championship, you’d be surprised of all the little things that come with it," he explained. "The things that are cool, the things that are not. The pros and cons to it.'

"So, just to be thrown in that conversation with a lot of New York athlete greats, I mean, it’s a real honor. It’s something I don’t take lightly. I would never proclaim myself that."

item.title: Trump floats an unexpected name to be his successor as powerhouses Rubio and Vance stand by
item.description: Donald Trump stunned the White House press briefing room by asking Stephen Miller if he wants to run for president, as JD Vance and Marco Rubio looked on.
item.content:encoded:
During a lighthearted Friday afternoon moment with the media inside the White House press briefing room, President Donald Trump floated a new name to succeed him as president, while two expected 2028 hopefuls stood by.

The president asked the media if they'd like to continue with the press conference — where Trump provided updates on his trip to China where he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This prompted laughs from Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who flanked him on either side during the briefing.

Then, he asked newly-minted Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, whom he called the "most powerful man in the world," to speak with members of the press.

MAGA VOTERS REVEAL WHO THEY WANT TO SEE LEAD GOP IN 2028

Miller took the podium and launched into a more than two-minute speech listing Trump's accomplishments from the first two years of his second term in office.

"I just wanted to say that what President Trump has achieved over the last two years is more than any president has achieved by far in American history. We can stand up here for four hours and go through achievement by achievement by achievement," Miller said.

He then rattled some of them off, including:

"Under his leadership, the next two years are going to be the greatest two years in American history," Miller said. "And I'm so proud to be his chief of staff to oversee on his behalf the staff in this building to keep delivering wins for this extraordinary American leader."

Trump was clearly impressed with Miller, who stepped in to replace Susie Wiles earlier this month following sweeping midterm losses for Republicans.

"We have breaking news! Breaking news!" Trump said. "He was better than these two guys," he added, turning towards Vance and Rubio, who both also spoke at the press conference.

"Do you want to run for president?" Trump asked Miller as he was leaving the podium, prompting laughter from the group.

STEPHEN MILLER'S INTERNAL MEMO UNLEASHES TRUMP AGENCIES AFTER 'ABSOLUTE CONTROL' UNDER WILES' REIGN

No major names from either party have yet to announce their intentions to run for president in 2028. But with the midterms finished, rumors have swirled about who will toss their hats in the ring.

Vance and Rubio are widely viewed as the two most viable options for Republicans.

Miller's name has not been previously floated as a contender for launching a White House bid.
